extracted.intended_audience: shippers/carriers and regulatory compliance officers in the radioactive material transport and packaging industry (including nuclear industry, medical/industrial isotope suppliers, NRC/DOT stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final-rule discussion harmonizing U.S. Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR) with IAEA TS-R-1/TS-G-1.1, covering packaging, testing, air transport, fissile exemptions, and transitional provisions for radioactive material shipments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermal test requirement for UF6 packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for thermal tests for packages designed to contain uranium hexafluoride (UF6) are necessary for domestic shipments in order to address potential increased societal risks from transport accidents involving fire and to achieve international harmonization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted large numbers of depleted UF6 cylinders and high overpack/transport costs if thermal protection requirements were incorporated; one recommended retaining current HMR requirements for five years. The agency concluded thermal tests are necessary despite commenter cost concerns because of safety and harmonization benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticality safety—water in-leakage assumption for UF6 packages (IAEA Para. 677(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: IAEA Paragraph 677(b) permits UF6 packages to be evaluated without assuming water leaks into the containment system if the packages satisfy specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule states this is not a relaxation of previous regulatory requirements but an enumeration of existing regulatory agency practices. Commenters argued the change would relax the requirement to show a single package is subcritical assuming water ingress; the agency disagreed, citing the IAEA provision and prior practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type C package performance standards for air transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Type C packages are designed to withstand severe accident conditions associated with air transport without loss of containment or significant increase in external radiation levels; they apply above specified activity thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type C thresholds: total activity above 3,000 A1 or 100,000 A2 (special form) or above 3,000 A2 for other material. Type C tests are more stringent than Type B: 90 m/s impact (vs 9-m drop for Type B) and a 60-minute fire test (vs 30-minute for Type B). These stringent tests aim to produce designs that survive more severe aircraft accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low Dispersible Material (LDM) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: LDM is an IAEA material exception for materials with limited dispersibility, solubility, and radiation such that they may be transported by air in Type B packages instead of Type C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LDM test requirements are a subset of Type C (90 m/s impact and 60-minute thermal test) plus a solubility test, performed on the material without packaging. LDM must have external radiation <10 mSv/h (1 rem/hr) at 3 meters. Specific acceptance criteria: less than 100 A2 in gaseous or particulate form of aerodynamic equivalent diameter <100 micrometers, and less than 100 A2 in solution. LDM must be certified by the Competent Authority (IAEA paragraphs cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency jurisdiction for fissile and greater-than-Type-A packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the DOT–NRC MOU, the NRC has responsibility for matters concerning packagings for fissile and greater-than-Type-A quantities of radioactive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. regulations do not contain Type C or LDM categories; NRC has specific air transport requirements for plutonium (10 CFR 71.64 and 71.74) that continue to apply. Because of the MOU, NRC's positions drive adoption for fissile packaging matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-adoption of IAEA Type C and LDM standards in HMR
rubrics_metrics.description: The DOT/RSPA (and NRC position) are not adopting the IAEA standards for Type C packaging or Low Dispersible Material in this final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters supported the proposal not to adopt these standards; RSPA follows NRC and will not adopt Type C/LDM concepts or issue Competent Authority Certificates for them at this time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of NRC fissile material exemption provisions (§173.453)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adopts the NRC's fissile material exemption provisions into §173.453 and incorporates revised NRC language for fissile material exceptions into the HMR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include adopting NRC exemptions, removing the definition for 'fissile material, controlled shipment,' revising §§173.457 and 173.459 to remove references, and establishing requirements for non-exclusive and exclusive use shipments of fissile material packages based on TS-R-1 package and conveyance CSI limits to simplify transport while maintaining criticality safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of the Type B(DP) package concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The NRC proposed a Type B(DP) package concept to be used for transporting and storing spent fuel, but the NRC withdrew reference to Type B(DP) in its final rule and DOT removed references accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the final HMR text has been revised to remove any references to a Type B(DP) package.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for guidance on criticality analyses for fissile materials by air
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested clarification and guidance for conducting criticality analyses for fissile materials shipped by air; suggested inclusion of a guidance note in TS-G-1.1 and harmonization with HMR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOT has no unilateral authority to change IAEA documents but will analyze problems in coordination with NRC and consider issuing guidance documents (e.g., in TS-G-1.1) if appropriate to address problems encountered in performing criticality analyses for air shipments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent Authority Certificate issuance policy for air transport (Type C/LDM)
rubrics_metrics.description: RSPA's Office of Hazardous Materials Safety, as the U.S. Competent Authority, does not intend to issue Certificates of Competent Authority for Type C packages or LDM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other Certificates of Competent Authority for international transport of fissile materials by air will be issued in accordance with §§173.471 and 173.473. DOT will not provide CA certificates for concepts it has not adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: General transitional requirements for packaging regulation changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional requirements typically authorize: (1) continued use of existing package designs and packagings already fabricated (possibly with additional requirements), (2) completion of packagings in fabrication within a specified period, and (3) limited modifications to package designs/packagings without demonstrating full compliance if modifications do not significantly affect safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each transition between IAEA editions and corresponding NRC/DOT revisions has contained transitional provisions; TS-R-1 transitional paragraphs 815–818 are referenced as the basis for impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for continued authorization of 1973/1973A-approved packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Packages approved based on Safety Series No. 6 (1973/1973A) may continue to be used through their design life provided specific conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (1) Multilateral approval obtained as applicable; (2) TS-R-1 quality assurance requirements adhered to; (3) TS-R-1 A1 and A2 activity values used; and (4) if applicable, approval for air transport of fissile radioactive material obtained. No new packagings may be fabricated to this design standard. If a safety issue is identified, the packaging must meet all applicable TS-R-1 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and sunset for 1985/1985A-approved packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Packages approved based on Safety Series No. 6 (1985/1985A) may continue to be used provided they meet TS-R-1 QA and A1/A2 requirements and, if applicable, air transport approvals; but use of these packages will end by specified dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use may continue and after Dec 31, 2003, use may continue under multilateral approval; if safety issues arise packaging must meet TS-R-1. Use of these packagings will end on Dec 31, 2006. Beginning Jan 1, 2007, all packages shipped internationally must meet TS-R-1 packaging approval requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-out policy for 1967-based package designs
rubrics_metrics.description: NRC concluded that packages approved under the 1967 IAEA regulations lack enhanced safety features and is phasing out package design certificates based on 1967 regulations; designs were categorized into five categories for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five categories: (1) designs that may meet current standards with no modifications but not yet submitted for review; (2) designs that can meet standards after minor changes; (3) spent fuel casks with stringent QA applied; (4) designs that cannot be shown to meet current standards; (5) designs with unknown safety performance. NRC will phase out designs that fall into categories 4 and 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition and transition timeline for older DOT Specification packages (6L, 6M, 20WC, 21WC)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOT proposed and the final rule prohibits new manufacture of DOT Specification 6L, 6M, 20WC and 21WC packages as of the effective date and phases out their use after a transition period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To provide time for adjustment, DOT doubled the transition period to four years from the effective date; the effective date is nine months after publication of the final rule, so affected parties will have approximately five years from publication to establish alternatives. Existing packages may continue only if shown to satisfy current performance requirements and are certified by NRC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revalidation requirement for foreign Competent Authority Certificates and imported Type B(U) packages
rubrics_metrics.description: DOT/NRC policy is that revalidations of foreign package design approvals should be made for import/export or domestic use only after U.S. authorities have assured packages meet U.S. safety standards; DOT will not accept foreign CA certificates without U.S. revalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter recommended accepting foreign competent authority certificates without U.S. revalidation; DOT disagreed, stating revalidation is required for safety reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of economic impacts and transition-period length for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory decisions on transition periods and phase-outs must consider economic impacts on small entities and the availability/cost/time to recertify or redesign packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided high cost estimates and urged grandfathering or longer transitions; DOT and NRC analyzed and estimated much lower realistic certification and manufacturing costs, concluded longer transitions were nonetheless warranted and extended the transition period. The agency weighed economic impacts but did not accept commenter cost estimates at face value.
